implementation_notes: The fallback mechanism is the language's own error model: catch the specific dependency failure (or test a C++17 std::optional result) and substitute a cached or reduced value, recording the mode in one place. What replaces the classic degraded-mode object is RAII plus a value type: unwinding releases the primary attempt's resources, so the substitute path only has to produce a value, and optional::value_or expresses "use the fallback if absent" without a flag. Choose the exception form when the failure is a real runtime dependency error; prefer returning std::optional where the absence is an expected, cheap outcome (lookup miss, no cached entry).
pitfalls: catch(...) also swallows programming errors (std::bad_alloc, std::logic_error): degrade only on the failure categories whose substitute is semantically valid.
The fallback runs inside the handler: if it can throw, the exception escapes the degraded path, so keep it simple and noexcept-safe.
A std::function fallback captured per request allocates and can dangle: keep the policy object owned by the component, not by the call.

variants.name: std::expected monadic fallback chain (C++23)
variants.implementation_notes: C++23's std::expected makes the fallback a value transformation instead of a control-flow jump: primary().or_else(cached).value_or(default) composes the substitute without try/catch and works in noexcept or exceptions-disabled builds. The roles are unchanged - what changes is that the degraded path is visible in the type and cannot be forgotten, because the caller must consume the expected value. Choose it where the toolchain is C++23 and a dependency failure is part of normal operation; keep the exception form where third-party code throws and you must catch at a boundary.
pitfalls: expected carries no context by default: record the reason before or_else collapses the error into the substitute.
or_else only fires for the error value - a default-constructed Report inside expected reads as "success with garbage", so fallbacks must produce genuinely valid values.
Monadic chains hide where the degradation happened; keep the metrics call inside the or_else lambda or the degraded path becomes invisible.
